pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** Choosing the Right Material

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y2 'Uses of everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "identify and compare the suitability of a variety of everyday materials, including wood, metal, plastic, glass, brick, rock, paper and cardboard for particular uses." Non-statutory guidance suggests pupils "think about the properties of materials that make them suitable or unsuitable for particular purposes" and are introduced to the people who developed useful new materials (John Dunlop, Charles Macintosh, John McAdam).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-2):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-2]." Clarification names strength, flexibility, hardness, texture, absorbency. DCI PS1.A: "Different properties are suited to different purposes." SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; CCC: Cause and Effect. (Asterisked — integrates engineering.)

- **Operational details:** Move children from describing a property to using it as a REASON for a choice. Anchor every judgement in the property→purpose link: glass for windows because it is transparent AND waterproof; wood for a chair because it is hard and rigid; wellies from waterproof plastic/rubber, not absorbent paper. Compare two candidate materials for one job and have the child justify the winner ('which is better for a raincoat — and why?'), then run the reverse ('why would paper be a poor choice?'). Use silly-material provocations (a chocolate teapot, a glass hammer) to force the property reasoning into the open. Connect to the inventor stories so children see material choice as a real human problem-solving act.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete → early reasoning). The child can explain why a named material suits a purpose using a property word, compare two materials for one use and justify the better choice, and suggest — with a reason — an alternative material for an object or explain why a given material would fail.
bestPractices: Always tie the choice to a property REASON ('glass because it is transparent'), never to familiarity or appearance alone.
Use head-to-head comparisons for a single purpose so children weigh one material against another rather than judging in isolation.
Deploy absurd-material provocations (chocolate teapot, paper umbrella, glass hammer) to make the property-suitability reasoning explicit and memorable.
Run the reasoning both ways — why a material suits a use AND why an alternative would fail — to deepen the property→function link.
Acknowledge that most objects balance SEVERAL properties (a saucepan must conduct heat, be hard, and not melt), so 'best' means best-on-balance, not perfect.
Use the inventor case studies (Dunlop, Macintosh, McAdam) to frame material choice as real problem-solving, per the DfE non-statutory guidance.
keyRepresentations: A property→purpose match board (materials ↔ jobs, justified by a property word)
Head-to-head 'which is better for this job?' comparison cards
Absurd-object provocations (chocolate teapot, glass hammer) for reasoning discussion
Real everyday objects labelled with the property that earns their material its job (wellies = waterproof; window = transparent)
Inventor mini-stories linking a new material to the problem it solved (Macintosh → waterproof coat)
commonMisconceptions: Choosing a material by familiarity or appearance ('cups are usually plastic') rather than by the property the job needs.
Believing there is one 'best' material for everything (often metal or plastic), instead of best-for-this-purpose.
Failing to link the property to the function — naming a material as suitable without saying which property makes it so.
Ignoring that objects often need SEVERAL properties at once, so judging on a single property and missing trade-offs.
Assuming a material's suitability is fixed by what it 'is' rather than reasoned from tested behaviour (a Y2→Y5 fair-test bridge).

learn.summary: For ages 6–8, teach children to justify material choices by the PROPERTY the job needs, not by habit or appearance: glass for windows because it is transparent and waterproof; boots from waterproof, flexible plastic/rubber; wood for a chair because it is hard and rigid. Move from naming a property to using it as a REASON, comparing two candidate materials head-to-head for one job, running the reasoning both ways (why this suits / why an alternative fails), and recognising that many objects need SEVERAL properties at once so 'best' means best-on-balance. Absurd-material provocations (chocolate teapot, glass hammer) and inventor case studies (Dunlop, Macintosh, McAdam) make the property→purpose reasoning explicit. Aligns to DfE KS1 Y2 'Uses of everyday materials' and NGSS 2-PS1-2.

activities.title: Kit out the job: choose a material and see if it works
feedback: If the paper coat soaked through: 'The paper let the rain through because it is absorbent — the coat's job is to keep rain out, so we need a waterproof material like plastic.'
If a child picks a material by looks: 'The shiny one looks nice, but what does the coat need to DO? Which material keeps the rain out?'

For the window trade-off: 'The metal kept the rain out but you couldn't see through it, and the cardboard went soggy and dark. Glass is transparent AND waterproof, so it does both jobs the window needs.'
Chocolate teapot (adult-run): 'It started to soften and melt when the warm water went in — chocolate melts when it gets warm, so it can't do a teapot's job.'
activities.rationale: Equipping an object and seeing it succeed or fail dramatises choice-with-consequence and is intended to supply the fail-then-fix feedback that may help consolidate the property→purpose link; testing candidate materials and judging which is best suited mirrors the NGSS 2-PS1-2 analysis verb. A hands-on or acted-out demonstration lets young learners experience the consequence rather than only recall the usual answer. Heat outcomes are adult-run for safety.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-2]'; DCI PS1.A 'Different properties are suited to different purposes'; CCC Cause and Effect.

DfE KS1 Y2 statutory requirement: 'identify and compare the suitability of a variety of everyday materials... for particular uses'; non-statutory 'properties that make them suitable or unsuitable'; inventors Dunlop/Macintosh/McAdam.
learnerActions: Pick an everyday object with a clear job — a rainy-day coat, an umbrella, a saucepan, a window, a boot.
Choose a material for it from a small set (e.g. paper, plastic, glass, cardboard, metal).
State out loud, before testing, which property you think matters and why you picked that material.

Observe or act out what happens when the object is used: pour water on the coat, let 'rain' hit the window. Any test involving heat (a saucepan near a hob, warm water on chocolate) is run by an adult as a demonstration, or acted out in pretend play — children do not hold materials near real heat.
Compare the result to your prediction: did the paper coat let the rain soak through? Did the plastic coat bead the drops off? Name the property that decided the outcome.
Watch the absurd choice (an adult pours warm water into a chocolate teapot) and describe what goes wrong and why.

For the window, compare glass (you can see out AND rain stays out) with a sheet of metal (rain stays out but it is dark — you cannot see through it), with cardboard (dark, and it goes soggy and lets water through), and with no material (wet) to discover that some jobs need TWO properties at once.
activities.intendedInsight: The right material rescues a job and the wrong one visibly lets it down, so a property is a REASON for a choice, not just a label; some jobs demand more than one property at once.

activities.title: Real objects and their earning property (reveal scene)
feedback: 'Wellies are made of rubber or plastic because it is waterproof — paper would soak up the puddle and your feet would get wet.'
'The window is glass because it is transparent — you can see out, and it is waterproof so rain stays out.'
activities.rationale: A reveal/flap scene is intended to teach the property→purpose link for early readers and can reinforce the reasoning, but it supports rather than leads because it does not stage the comparative decision or the fail-case the way an active trial does.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 statutory requirement: 'identify and compare the suitability of a variety of everyday materials... for particular uses'; non-statutory 'properties that make them suitable or unsuitable'; inventors Dunlop/Macintosh/McAdam.
learnerActions: Look at real everyday objects or an illustrated home/street scene (window, coat, saucepan, book, wellies).
For each object, name the one property that earns its material its job — e.g. 'wellies — plastic — WATERPROOF so your feet stay dry'.
Then consider 'what if it were made of paper?' and say why that would fail.
Handle or examine the real objects where possible to connect the property word to how the material behaves.
activities.intendedInsight: Every object around us was made from a material chosen for the property its job needs, and swapping in the wrong material reveals why that property mattered.

activities.title: Which is better for this job — and why? (head-to-head)
feedback: Raincoat, plastic vs paper: 'Plastic wins because it is waterproof; paper would fail because it is absorbent and would soak through.'
Glass hammer: 'A hammer needs to be hard and tough — glass is hard but brittle, so it would be likely to crack or shatter when it hit something.'
If a child names only one property for a boot: 'Good — it's waterproof. A boot also has to bend as you walk, so what else does the material need to be? (flexible).'
activities.rationale: Head-to-head comparison and reverse reasoning are intended to deepen the property→function link; matching, sorting and 'which is better, why' tasks let children practise and can surface specific reasoning errors through the wrong options offered. These check the conclusion, so pair them with active trials that let children experience the choice.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 statutory requirement: 'identify and compare the suitability of a variety of everyday materials... for particular uses'; non-statutory 'properties that make them suitable or unsuitable'; inventors Dunlop/Macintosh/McAdam.
Documented KS1/2 misconceptions: choosing materials by familiarity/appearance not property; belief in one universally 'best' material; failure to link property to function.
learnerActions: Take one job (a raincoat, a drinking cup, a hammer) and two candidate materials.
Decide which material is better for that job and SAY the property that makes it win.
Run the reasoning in reverse: explain why the other material would be a poor choice.
Sort a small set of materials into 'suitable' and 'unsuitable' for a named job, giving a property reason for each.
Spot the silly material in a set (e.g. a glass hammer among metal tools) and explain what would go wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging two materials against each other for one purpose forces you to weigh a property against a need, which is stronger than judging a single material in isolation.

activities.title: The inventor's problem (material choice as problem-solving)
feedback: 'Macintosh needed something rain couldn't get through — he used rubberised fabric because it is waterproof.'
If the child says 'paper' for the coat: 'Would paper keep the rain out? Why not? What property do we need instead?'
activities.rationale: Inventor case studies frame material choice as genuine problem-solving per DfE non-statutory guidance. A brief in-role designer prompt can draw out justification, but young children cannot sustain long open dialogue, so keep exchanges short and pair talk with trying materials.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 statutory requirement: 'identify and compare the suitability of a variety of everyday materials... for particular uses'; non-statutory 'properties that make them suitable or unsuitable'; inventors Dunlop/Macintosh/McAdam.
learnerActions: Hear a short story of an inventor who solved a real problem with a material: Charles Macintosh and the waterproof coat, John Dunlop and the air-filled (pneumatic) rubber tyre, John McAdam and road surfacing made of layers of crushed stone.
Say what problem the inventor faced and which property of the material they chose solved it.
Take on a design brief in role — e.g. 'I need a coat that keeps the rain out' — choose a material and justify it, answering 'why not paper?' follow-up prompts.
Keep turns short; speak or act out the justification rather than writing long answers.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a material is a real human problem-solving act: an inventor matches a material's property to the job that needs doing.

constraints: Always tie the choice to a property REASON ('glass because it is transparent'), never to familiarity or appearance alone.

Most objects balance SEVERAL properties (a saucepan must conduct heat, be hard, and not melt; a boot must be waterproof AND flexible), so 'best' means best-on-balance, not perfect; check the material against every job the object must do.

Reveal/flap scenes and matching or sorting tasks assess or reinforce the conclusion; they do not by themselves let a child experience the choice and its consequence, so use them alongside an active trial, not as the sole activity.
A fixed picture or sorting task can still teach the property→purpose link, but it does not by itself stage the fail-then-fix moment that an acted-out or hands-on trial provides.
In-role dialogue suits short, audio-supported turns for this age; do not expect sustained open discussion from 6–8s.
Any heat demonstration (saucepan near a hob, melting chocolate, warm water) must be adult-run and supervised; children do not handle materials near real heat.

Suitability reasoning is mainly about matching a property to a purpose rather than spatial manipulation, so added depth/3D is optional here — this is a scoped observation, not a claim that spatial media can never help.
This is an early-reasoning checkpoint (concrete → early reasoning); fair-testing of materials to decide suitability is a later bridge (Y2→Y5), not required here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-review softened remaining efficacy claims in the reveal-scene and head-to-head rationales to intended/may wording and removed residual quiz-step vocabulary ('distractors', 'quiz-style') from the guidance.

The original catalog claims that 'only live recompute delivers' the success/failure feedback, that a quiz 'only assesses', and that 3D 'adds nothing' are fit opinions, not established pedagogical facts; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits. A fixed image or sorting task can still teach; an interactive trial offers a different (consequence-showing) experience.
The STEM Learning misconceptions source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its misconception list as indicative, not confirmed.
Heat/melting outcomes (chocolate softening, materials near heat) depend on the specific setup, must be demonstrated safely by an adult, and are typical rather than guaranteed for every arrangement.

assess.poeTask: Offer to make a tiny teapot (or cup) from chocolate. Ask the child to PREDICT whether it will work when you pour warm water in, and to say WHY before you pour. Many predict it's fine ('it's a cup shape'). Pour warm water: the chocolate softens and leaks. The reason given beforehand is the diagnostic part — a child reasoning from properties predicts failure ('chocolate melts when it's warm') while a child reasoning from shape/appearance is surprised.
probeDeeper: What does this object need to DO — what's the most important property for that job?
Could we make it from newspaper? Why would that fail?
A saucepan is metal but its handle is often plastic — why a different material for the handle?
Which matters more for a raincoat: that it's your favourite colour, or that it's waterproof?
assess.correctAnswer: Matches the property to the purpose: boots are plastic/rubber because they are waterproof AND flexible (bend as you walk, keep feet dry); a chocolate teapot fails because chocolate melts with hot water. Reasons from the property the job needs, not from habit or looks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Justifies by familiarity/convention, not property — 'windows are glass because windows are always glass'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to function: 'what does this object need to DO?' — list the jobs, then ask which property meets each; the choice follows from the property.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because boots are always made of rubber — that's just what boots are.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-2 yields no property, only 'that's how it is' or 'that's what they're made of'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses by appearance/aesthetics rather than function — 'the shiny metal one because it looks strong and nice'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a good-looking but unsuitable option with a plain suitable one (a smart paper cup vs a plain plastic one for holding water); function beats looks.
errorPatterns.distractor: The metal one, because it looks strong and shiny.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Bases the choice on looks and ignores the property the job actually needs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Single-property tunnel vision — justifies with one property and ignores that many uses need two (a boot must be waterproof AND flexible; a window transparent AND rigid AND weatherproof).
errorPatterns.nextMove: For one object, list ALL the jobs it must do and check the material against each; reconnect to grouping materials by more than one property.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives one property and is stumped when the use clearly needs more than one.

responseLevels.gap: Justifies a choice by habit, colour or 'that's what it's made of'; no property reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Matches property to purpose with reasoning, weighs more than one requirement where the use needs it, and evaluates an alternative material by its properties.
responseLevels.partial: Names one relevant property for the obvious case but can't weigh competing requirements or evaluate an alternative material.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Wellington boots are made of rubber or plastic. Someone says it's just because boots are always made of that. What's the REAL reason we pick that material for boots — what does the material need to do?' Then: 'I want to make a teapot. Would glass, metal or chocolate be a bad choice — and why?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-2 'why' separates a child who reasons from familiarity ('that's just what it's made of') from one who names the property the purpose demands. Introducing an alternative or absurd material forces genuine property reasoning rather than recall of the usual answer.
